rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression suppresses a governing noun, understood as God's assault, punishment, or grasp; the Banū Naḍīr's forts falsely seemed to protect them from human attack and divine power.
rows.anchor: immune from human onslaughts, but also from the grasp of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording stresses that God came upon the people from a direction they could not imagine.
rows.anchor: God came upon them from where they could not even imagine.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God struck the Banū Naḍīr by casting terror into their hearts, without needing to dismantle their fortifications; terror drove them to wreck their own houses.
rows.anchor: they were so terror-struck that they rampaged the houses they constructed with their own hands.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Real strength comes from faith in God within the heart, not from weapons or fortress walls; weapons without that strength may even destroy their owners.
rows.anchor: real power does not reside in weapons or in the walls of forts; it resides in the hearts and is engendered by faith in God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the people destroying their houses presents the scene as if it were unfolding before the sūrah's audience.
rows.anchor: portrays the situation as if it was occurring before the addresses of the sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given permission to carry away what they could manage on camels, they pulled out building materials; greed and hostility also led them to ruin what they left for the Muslims.
rows.anchor: Taking advantage of this permission, they tried to pullout the logs, joints, doors and windows to take with them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers' hands suggest that Muslims helped the Banū Naḍīr's dismantling to hasten their departure; later verses also show Muslims cutting some trees for wartime needs.
rows.anchor: it is evident from some succeeding verses that Muslims struck down some of their trees for war needs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage urges anyone capable of reflection to take a lesson from the expulsion.
rows.anchor: urge all people who can seek a lesson to learn a lesson

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Satan-like betrayal evokes Badr: the Jews, Islahi says, conspired by inciting the Quraysh and promising support, then disowned them when the battle came.
rows.anchor: the battle of Badr took place because of a conspiracy of the Jews. It is they who incited the Quraysh and planned the onslaught for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an elsewhere depicts sinners blaming satanic leaders at Judgement, while those leaders deny control and say followers chose their own deeds and must face the consequences.
rows.anchor: the sinners will try to hold their satanic leaders responsible for their crimes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's worldly agents similarly lure people into sin, then try to evade responsibility when its consequences arrive.
rows.anchor: they allure people into sin, but when the consequences come, they try to save themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After a crime, self-exculpation and blaming others help neither party: both wrongdoers end in Hell forever.
rows.anchor: trying to save one’s own skin and blaming others for it has no benefit for either party

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the closing passage addresses Muslims generally, its context directs it especially to the hypocrites discussed from the sūrah's beginning.
rows.anchor: Though, by the words used, they address common Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its central warning is to examine one's preparation for the imminent Day of Accountability, knowing that God sees every deed and will recompense it.
rows.anchor: serious consideration is the nature and extent of his preparation for the day of accountability

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who forget God only injure themselves, becoming blind to their own good, evil, and ultimate fate, as the Jews had been.
rows.anchor: Those who forget Him, harm Him in no way; they, in fact, become blind to their own good and evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference between the people of Paradise and Hell is enormous: Paradise's people alone succeed, while the rest face eternal loss.
rows.anchor: Only the dwellers of Paradise will attain success and salvation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's mountain parable shows the truth has been fully conveyed; a mountain would break from fear, exposing the hypocrites' hard-heartedness.
rows.anchor: been revealed on a mountain, it would have been crushed to pieces because of God’s fear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should reflect on God's attributes and bring their inner and outward lives, beliefs, deeds, and hoped-for outcome into harmony with them.
rows.anchor: they should assess and evaluate their present and future, their good and evil, their beliefs and deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though phrased for all believers, the verse is aimed primarily at the hypocrites whose weaknesses the sūrah has exposed.
rows.anchor: their context and placement show that they are directed primarily at the hypocrites whose weaknesses are under discussion from the beginning of this sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fundamental remedy for spiritual, intellectual, and moral illness is attention to the reality of accountability; believers must assess their deeds for the coming Judgement.
rows.anchor: Believers should continue to asses what deeds they have done in preparation of the imminent Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to fear God counters the idea that worldly amusement simply ends; this life is followed by certain reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: this world is a place of merriment and amusement which will suddenly end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tomorrow” signifies the Hereafter's nearness and certainty, so people must not defer self-accountability.
rows.anchor: The Hereafter is signified by the word “tomorrow.” The reason is to refer to its proximity and certainty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the command to fear God emphasizes its importance and reminds people that God knows every word and deed and will repay them.
rows.anchor: repeated in order to direct attention to the importance of the issue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting God makes people indifferent to their own good, evil, and fate; life is meant for obedience and earning the eternal kingdom, not brief luxury.
rows.anchor: All value, significance and majesty of life depends on understanding the reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life is a purposeful gift from a gracious Lord: living by its purpose brings eternal reward, while forgetting it makes life a curse for oneself.
rows.anchor: He has given it with a special purpose. If a person leads his life in accordance with this special purpose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting God means forgetting one's relationship with Him and becoming defiant, which is why such people are called the truly disobedient.
rows.anchor: these people are the real disobedient of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True remembrance keeps one's relationship with God continually present; remembrance reduced to ritual has little effect.
rows.anchor: a person should always keep fresh before himself the nature of his relationship with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise and Hell differ by eternal mercy versus eternal doom, not by a small degree that base desires can safely disregard.
rows.anchor: the difference between the two is that of eternal doom and eternal mercy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountain's imagined submission rebukes hypocrites: a hard mountain would break from God's fear, yet their hearts remain unaffected by the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: so hard-hearted are the hypocrites that they are not even slightly effected by it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable asks readers to see that if the Qur'an does not move them, the fault is their callousness; God may seal their hearts as He did the Jews'.
rows.anchor: the fault does not lie with it; it lies with their callous hearts.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews' hearts are compared to rocks, some of which split or fall in fear of God, while the hypocrites are warned against becoming similarly hardened.
rows.anchor: some which break asunder and water gushes from them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says his mentor Farāhī interprets this verse alongside the trust offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains; Islahi treats that as one aspect and also invokes texts on hardened hearts.
rows.anchor:
It is evident from certain clues referred to by my mentor, Im ām Ḥamīd al-D īn
Farāhī that he interprets this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an itself calls the mountain comparison a parable; parables make abstract matters tangible without exaggeration or fantasy.
rows.anchor: In a parable, there is no exaggeration or fantasy to be found

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may be general or may comfort the Prophet: if his audience is unmoved, the failure lies in their hearts, not his call.
rows.anchor: if people are not being influenced by his call, then this is no fault of his

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning fear of God, the passage names His attributes so believers, disbelievers, and hypocrites can understand how to fear, love, hope in, trust, and serve Him.
rows.anchor: so that the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites, all come to know of these attributes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attributes of God and their implications form the basis of religion and sharīʿah; Qur'anic commands are manifestations of them, so full understanding requires the whole Qur'an.
rows.anchor: the basis of the sharī‘ah and religion is the attributes of God and what these attributes entail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone is deity and worthy of worship, so people should turn to Him in hope and despair rather than treating another as the source of answered prayers.
rows.anchor: no one except Him is God. For this reason, a person should turn to him in both hope and despair.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows everything hidden or apparent to people; this grounds both fear of being called to account and hope in entrusting pleas to Him.
rows.anchor: whatever a person does, whether openly or secretly, it is in God’s knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God knows all, no one can conceal words or deeds at Judgement or gain an unjust intercession; people should entrust their pleas to Him.
rows.anchor: neither will a person be able to hide any of his words or deeds, nor will any intercessor wrongly intercede for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān conveys the fervor of God's mercy, while al-Raḥīm conveys its continuity and permanence; both attributes combine hope and fear.
rows.anchor: The former alludes to the fervour and zeal found in God’s mercy, and the latter to its continuity and permanence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God is merciful, He will not oppress anyone; that same mercy requires Judgement so He can avenge oppression and give everyone justice.
rows.anchor: it is this mercy which necessitates such a day to come so that He does justice with each and every person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating that God alone is deity stresses monotheism and refutes shirk, which arises from false ideas about the attributes on which religion rests.
rows.anchor: the refutation of polytheism and the affirmation of monotheism is the most important thing pointed out here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eight successive attributes have no conjunction between them, indicating that they are all simultaneously present in the one they qualify.
rows.anchor: when attributes are mentioned in this way, without any particle of conjugation, then it means that they are simultaneously present in the noun they qualify.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As al-Malik, God alone created, owns, and rules the world; His sovereignty entitles Him to send messengers with directives for people to obey.
rows.anchor: He alone created the world and He alone is its master and ruler.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Quddūs means God is free of blemish, shortcoming, and wrong.
rows.anchor: He is devoid of any blemish, any shortcoming and any wrong.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God is pure and perfect, He sent His Book and messengers to purify His servants; Sūrah al-Jumuʿah states the same attributes and their entailments.
rows.anchor: He sent His messengers so that people can become worthy of His nearness by being cleansed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Salām means peace, happiness, and serenity; God shelters His servants from calamity, and refuge in Him brings contentment.
rows.anchor: In other words, God is a refuge and shield for His servants against every calamity and danger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God brings peace and tranquility to hearts.
rows.anchor: remembering God is a means of peace and tranquillity for the hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Muʾmin means the one who grants refuge: God protects anyone seeking refuge from Satan, and no one else can provide this refuge.
rows.anchor: when a person seeks His refuge against Satan and his agents, He grants him His refuge.

rows.speaker: Khalīl and Abū ‘Ubaydah
rows.claim: Khalīl and Abū ʿUbaydah understand al-Muhaymin to mean “guardian.”
rows.anchor: In the opinion of Khalīl and Abū ‘Ubaydah, this word means “guardian.”

rows.speaker: Ibn al-Anbārī
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī understands al-Muhaymin to mean “protector,” one who cares for people.
rows.anchor: Ibn al-Anb ārī is of the view that it means “protector”

rows.speaker: Imām Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī understands al-Muhaymin as one who can be trusted and acts as an advocate.
rows.anchor: Imām Farāhī25 says that it means “one who can be trusted and is one’s advocate.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi sees little difference among guardian, protector, and trusted advocate.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, there is not much difference between these meanings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is itself al-Muhaymin because it guards the other divine scriptures.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān is also al-Muyahmin because it is a guardian over all other divine scriptures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzīz means inaccessible and beyond, as well as powerful: none can overpower or dominate God.
rows.anchor: none can dominate or overpower God. He can vanquish all.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jabbār denotes might and power and can also refer to tall palm stalks; the Qur'an uses it for the formidable people feared by the Israelites.
rows.anchor: In the Qur’ ān, it has also been used for the formidable people, fearing whom, the Israelites had pleaded thus to the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jabbār refutes concepts of divinity that assign all significance to goddesses.
rows.anchor: This attribute refutes all those concepts of divinity, in which all significance is given to goddesses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mutakabbir is rightful greatness: anyone but God who claims inherent superiority is wrong, since all others receive their status from God; His own greatness is eternal.
rows.anchor: none except God has attained greatness and superiority on His own.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed scripture describes God as jealous of exclusive devotion; Islahi equates its term ghayūr with Qur'anic al-Mutakabbir.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, what the Qur’ ān has denoted by the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's majestic, perfect attributes make comparison with idols impossible; associating partners conflicts with His attributes and creates disharmony among them.
rows.anchor: what is the comparison between these attributes of majesty and perfection of the Almighty, and between these imaginary deities of the idolaters?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation unfolds in a first phase of design and planning, termed khalq.
rows.anchor: The first phase is that of design and plan. The Arabic word used for it is ﺧﻠﻖ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second phase brings a planned thing into existence, termed barʾ.
rows.anchor: The second phase is to bring it into existence. The Arabic word used for it is ﺑﺮء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third phase perfects and models the thing, termed taṣwīr.
rows.anchor: The third phase is to perfect it. The Arabic word used for it is ﺗﺼﻮﻳﺮ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God alone carries out all phases of creation without help, He alone deserves glorification and worship.
rows.anchor: He alone is worthy of being glorified and worshipped by all.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names mentioned are basic divine attributes, and every other beautiful name of God also expresses an attribute He possesses.
rows.anchor: All names of God express one or the other attribute He possesses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God creates all things, everything in heaven and earth glorifies Him; a person who refuses by choice rejects truth arrogantly and should worship God alone.
rows.anchor: this is an act of not acknowledging the truth, and arrogance on his part.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending recalls God's opening attributes: He has power to compel worship, but in wisdom grants humans free will to test whether they recognize His right or serve Satan.
rows.anchor: He wanted to test whether, after being granted with this status, he recognises the right of God on him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Munāfiqūn supplements al-Jumuʿah, whose ending exposed people who professed faith but abandoned the Friday sermon when a trade caravan arrived to pursue worldly interests.
rows.anchor: if a trade caravan would arrive, they would run towards it, abandoning the Prophet (sws) while he would be delivering the Friday sermon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites lack resolve to fulfill faith's requirements but want the Prophet's esteem, so they repeatedly swear that they regard him as God's Messenger.
rows.anchor: they would repeatedly swear before the Prophet (sws) that they regard him as a Messenger of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God declares the hypocrites liars; their conduct shows they disbelieve, and they use their oaths as a shield for hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: They use their oaths as a shield, and hide their hypocrisy behind it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Love of wealth and life caused the hypocrites to turn back from faith; God sealed their hearts and deprived them of understanding and reflection.
rows.anchor: The love of wealth and life has led them to withdraw the step they had taken towards faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first eight verses expose the hypocrites' character and identify their real illness as infatuation with worldly life.
rows.anchor: The first section which consists of eight verses discusses the character of the hypocrites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing three verses warn Muslims not to let wealth and children distract from remembering God; those who fail to spend for God's cause will regret it after death, when regret is useless.
rows.anchor: If, today, they would not properly benefit from their wealth by spending it for the cause of God, they will regret it once their life ends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first section identifies worldly love as the root of hypocrisy; the second urges Muslims to guard against that same cause.
rows.anchor: the first section points to the real reason for the hypocrisy, and the second emphatically urges Muslims to guard themselves from it.
